newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Just one big Argentine bank still in local hands.
newsitem.headline: Just one big Argentine bank still in local hands.

text.p: The Argentine banking landscape has changed dramatically in the last two weeks with just one of the country's top 10 private banks now remaining in local hands.

Banking giant HSBC Holdings Plc rounded off the recent buying spree Friday by announcing it will purchase all of the local Roberts Group, including Banco Roberts, for between $600 million and $688 million. "It is not an easy market to enter any more. Everybody is here now," said Esteban Thomsen, chief economist at ING Barings in Buenos Aires.
The purchases started two weeks ago when Spain's Banco de Bilbao Viscaya's Argentine-controlled Banco Frances bought 71.8 percent of retail bank Banco de Credito Argentino for $466 million.
Earlier this week, Spain's Banco Santander SA said it would buy 35.06 percent of Banco Rio for $594 million, giving it voting control.
As the dust settles, the focus in the financial district of Buenos Aires has shifted firmly to Banco de Galicia, the last large local bank with no major foreign shareholders.
Indeed, some see Galicia as the biggest prize of all. It is clearly the largest of the local private banks in terms of deposits.

According to central bank figures, its deposits totaled $3.9 billion and its loan portfolio $4.1 billion in February. Its closest competitor, Rio, had $3.0 billion in deposits and $3.5 billion in loans. Frances had $2.0 billion in deposits and Credito $1.6 billion.
Local markets were also speculating Friday that Canada's Bank of Novia Scotia could increase its 25 percent stake in Banco Quilmes.

But for all the frenzy, Banco Galicia may not end in the hands of foreigners. "I do not see any urgency," for it to go seeking foreign partners, said Thomsen. "It is a well established bank," with a large branch network.
"Nobody can say whether all banks will end in foreign hands," said Sergio Galvan, the head of research at Bansud.
High hopes are held by consumers and especially small and medium-sized companies that they will get access to cheaper credit and see banking costs fall as efficiency in the sector rises.

But, just weeks after the annual conference of the Argentine Banking Association at which inefficiencies in the banking system and still very high lending rates were highlighted, analysts did not see immediate effects of the sharpened competition in the market.
"This is not a one day process. Banking costs will not fall just yet," said Galvan.

Merging the operations of Credito and Frances, for instance, could take months as the two already have overlapping functions, with branch offices in many parts of the capital situated as close as just blocks apart.

Some analysts suggested Santander's Rio may be better placed to reap returns from its buyout because it does not need to merge any consumer banking operations. Santander's existing operations in Argentina concentrate on the brokerage business. It is also active in pension funds.
However, when these buy-outs start paying off they could bring home big profits to the foreign parent companies.

"Everyone is going to be a winner here," said Galvan, because the overseas institutions have bought into a market where the total pie of banking activities is expanding, as opposed to the mature markets in Western Europe or the U.S.
And Thomsen pointed out the expansion is not just one of consumer banking, but within the entire financial services industry, ranging from pensions to medical insurance.
HSBC's purchase of the entire Roberts group which includes insurance, pensions and healthcare as well as the retail and investment banking operations, exemplified that.
((--Buenos Aires Newsroom, 541 318-0668))
